name: Neuromuscular junction
summary: The chemical synapse between a motor axon terminal and a skeletal muscle fiber. Acetylcholine released in quanta from the terminal crosses the cleft, binds nicotinic receptors on the folded post-synaptic membrane to produce an end-plate potential and a muscle action potential, and is hydrolysed by acetylcholinesterase. Disease of the junction produces fatigable weakness without sensory loss, wasting or reflex change: post-synaptic antibodies in myasthenia gravis, pre-synaptic calcium-channel antibodies in the Lambert–Eaton syndrome, and toxins (botulinum, organophosphates, neuromuscular blockers) at various steps.

anatomy.location: Motor end plates near the middle of each muscle fiber where the terminal branches of the motor axon end; one junction per fiber, many per motor unit.

subdivisions.name: Presynaptic terminal
subdivisions.note: voltage-gated calcium channels, acetylcholine vesicles; target of Lambert–Eaton antibodies and botulinum toxin

subdivisions.name: Synaptic cleft
subdivisions.note: acetylcholinesterase in the basal lamina; target of organophosphates and pyridostigmine

subdivisions.name: Postsynaptic membrane
subdivisions.note: junctional folds with nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and MuSK; target of myasthenia gravis antibodies and of non-depolarizing blockers

function: Reliable one-to-one transmission of the motor neuron action potential to the muscle fiber with a large safety factor, which disease erodes to produce fatigability.

bestView.label: cervical cord; the junction is in the muscles, not imaged

imaging.normalAppearance: Not imaged directly. The imaging task in junction disease is the thymus: CT of the chest for thymoma or hyperplasia in myasthenia gravis, and a search for small-cell lung cancer in the Lambert–Eaton syndrome.

pathology.finding: Anterior mediastinal soft-tissue mass; thymic hyperplasia in younger patients.

pathology.pathology: Small-cell lung cancer in Lambert–Eaton syndrome
pathology.finding: Central lung mass with mediastinal nodes; repeat imaging for two years if negative.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Chest CT; repetitive nerve stimulation and single-fiber EMG; antibody testing

lesionEffects.deficit: Fatigable ptosis, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia and proximal weakness worse through the day
Proximal leg weakness that improves briefly with exercise, dry mouth, absent reflexes that return after exercise
Descending paralysis with dilated pupils and dry mouth
Weakness with fasciculations, salivation and miosis

examination: Sustained up-gaze for ptosis, repeated arm abduction, count to 50 for dysarthria
Ice pack test on a ptotic lid
Reflexes: normal in myasthenia, absent then facilitated in Lambert–Eaton
Pupils: normal in myasthenia, dilated in botulism
Respiratory function (vital capacity, single breath count)
pearls: Fluctuating weakness with normal sensation and normal reflexes is the junction
Never give aminoglycosides or magnesium to a myasthenic without thinking; check vital capacity, not oxygen saturation, in a myasthenic crisis
